title: FAA issues national ground stop – lifted 4.5 hours later (nbcnews.com)
comments:
For those interested, there was a 2009 outage of the FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure that at a surface level seems like it could be a similar failure mode. At the very least, it is an interesting read on how the FAAs systems operate, since a lot of the discussion so far has been wild speculation from people with little knowledge on how the national airspace system actually operates: https://www.oig.dot.gov/library-item/29670Of particular note is this section:
Risks of FTI Outages for Existing Operational Services 
As of December 2009, Harris reported that there are a total of 20,982 services operating on the FTI network. While FAA has transitioned all 1,808 IP services supporting FAA flight plans to the new FTI fiber optic network, additional risks will be introduced when the Agency begins transitioning other FAA services, such as En Route Automation Modernization (ERAM) and NextGen platforms, which also require IP technology to operate. Moreover, there are 19,174 existing services that may be transitioned to the new FTI fiber optic network. According to FAA, transitioning these remaining services is important because FTI now connects older FAA systems that provide safety-critical voice and surveillance radar information by utilizing Time Division Multiplex (TDM) technology, instead of IP services.reply

TBH TDM is far superior and it’s sad that the world discarded it. Packet switching is the worst thing to ever happen to phone calls.  Kids today have no idea how good it used to be (albeit at $0.50/min).reply

How do you "overload" a TDM system? It's just a multiplexer that turns one wideband link into N lower bandwidth links by bitwise interleaving. You can't "overload" it.
Whatever assigns links might be overloaded, and that's usually something like a telephone switch.There's an unverified mention of a fiber cut, which might result in fewer circuits being available. That usually returns an "all circuits busy" signal.None of the explanations will make sense until they stop coming from unqualified political appointees.reply
It's probably not TDM end to end nowadays. If they're backhauling it via MPLS or similar then loss of fiber capacity might render the legacy link inoperable.reply
I mean the fidelity of modern mics/converters/codecs in devices now is much better, but ya the tradeoff of VoIP is latency/jitter/dropouts etcreply

TDM only implies (in the traditional 8-bit framing format, at least) that you're giving a 64 kbps timeslot to a caller. You can put any arbitrary payload in there, like AAC, Opus, or whatever. Preferably a codec without an intrinsic lookahead delay though. You can bond multiple 64k timeslots too.Glad someone else appreciates circuit switched technologies though :) . It really does shine in any application that isn't burst-y data transfers.reply
has there been work on good real time audio codecs? I wonder how good you can do if you limit yourself to a latency of <1 sample?reply
It was painful not having full duplex calls for so long.reply

I love this work and everything else Ratatui does but I have to ask: if you're changing the terminal protocol and the terminal itself to do this, why not do something more ambitious; a full monospaced information-dense UI framework, a terminal designed for user interfaces, rather than one designed to replicate the limitations of dumb terminals?reply

Yep,and I want to do that too :)I've written about it before, but in brief the mountain of standards is worth ripping out wholesale and doing write as a semantic protocol. It's needed to solve several things that work really poorly in terminals because their unit of compatibility is cells rather than a higher primitive. It's hard to bake something on top that works well.The need is most strong in Accessibility, Text wrapping, Scrollback handling (i.e. making the scrollback editable and not dead text), and various other bits that make writing highly functional TUIs. Coding agents tend to find all those edge cases.This often gets push back that it's easy, to which I can point nay sayers at the various many months long issues on things in Codex, Gemini, Claude etc. on flickering, scrolling, key handline, IME, ... doing anything moderately complex involves modeling a terminal in a terminal app effectively.Ghostty and Rex sort of do the opposite bit. If you think of  it like a stack, they write a new layer underneath that transports the cells on a better multiplexer layer 0. I think a new semantic layer 2 is an approach that would be neat to work with.reply

>Barely enough time for the domain to resolve!contrary to popular belief, DNS doesn't actually need 24 hours (or whatever) to "propagate". It only needs enough time for caches to expire, if they exist. For non-existent domains this shouldn't be an issue.reply

Aside from regular caches (that use TTLs), there can also be a replication delay between primary master and secondary master servers.You make your changes to the zone file on the primary server. The secondary replicates the zone file (a "zone transfer") and uses its copy to serve requests, enabling you to have multiple authoritative servers.In the old days, the secondary server simply polled the primary server at a fixed interval to see if its zone data was out of date. It could potentially be hours if that's the schedule you chose. It wasn't uncommon to restart the secondary servers by hand if you needed something to propagate faster.Later, more sophisticated stuff was added like incremental zone transfers and the ability for the primary to send a notification to the secondary instead of relying only on polling. Those made it more practical to replicate quickly.There were scenarios back in the day when quick replication wasn't worth the cost. The primary and secondary servers might be on opposite sides of a 9600 baud modem connection where zone transfers would eat up a significant portion of available bandwidth.TLDR: DNS "propagation" is real, not a myth. It's just that today it's pretty trivial to make the propagation delay so tiny that it's negligible.reply

comments: > The fan downloads its root CA cert over plain HTTP. It was always MitM-able.The most fascinating part of this wave of LLM reverse engineering is seeing how many weird and poor choices were lying in plain sight.Any number of people could have discovered and exploited this, but it’s tedious work. Most people who can do this are busy with their job and other things. Now LLMs enable people who understand these things to quickly get through the tedious parts, so they can do a lot more of this work in their free time than they could before.reply

> The most fascinating part of this wave of LLM reverse engineering is seeing how many weird and poor choices were lying in plain sight.

I think what's interesting is that for decades one group of devs has been pushing for higher quality and security while other groups have been pushing for "good enough" or "MVP"[0]. Clearly the group that rushed won.But in some weird way we're coming to the day of reckoning. I'm sure we'll always have missed bugs but with a lot of what we're seeing it more seems like these were avoidable problems. Code issues I can easily imagine at least one person on the team said "this isn't acceptable, we need to correct it" and them getting overruled. I'm sure each and every one of you has seen, if not experienced, this.It'll be interesting to see if that continues. I suspect companies will still rush but from my experience even the best models happily produce shoddy code. And there's a feedback loop, the model's performance is influenced by the code's quality. So it's easy to degrade and get into a bad feedback loop. But I think people still value speed over quality, even in this world where Microsoft shit the bed[0] in quotes because the entire conversation is essentially about what is actually good enough and what actually is the minimum viable product.reply

I don't think it's fair to say that those who didn't push for more security pushed against it or just for good enough. They didn't care enough to push back, sure, they were coerced - maybe, they did wrong - probably. But there is a good enough in security too. If you want near-perfect security, keep if off the web. 
Don't get me wrong, I wish all products had minimal care for good practices, but I won't expect it the random Chinese made product.reply

> "Clearly the group that rushed won"This is has been the case since I started developing software in the 90's. As far as I, and likely many others, are concerned it might as well be a Software Aphorism.I think it will be very interesting as we continue to reverse engineer such things to find out just how poorly "glued together" the Paper Tigers really are....reply

"The fan downloads its root CA cert over plain HTTP"Would love to understand the decision-making behind this at Coway (or their firmware contractor). Anyone care to guess why someone would make this choice?reply

Hardware companies by and large don't get software. They just don't understand it. Their world is sourcing parts and assembly and packaging. They look at software like any other line item in the BOM: Like a screw or gasket. You source it from the cheapest supplier, and spoon it onto the product somewhere on the assembly line. These companies simply don't care about their software, and their requirements to their supplier amount to "make something work." The quality bar is literally "customer should not return the product."reply

> Anyone care to guess why someone would make this choice?My guess: At some point in the past, a firmware was developed without plans to include firmware update functionality. The team that did this was later burned when the client tried to use a new certificate that the hardcoded, unchangeable system didn't recognize.Angry meetings occurred, developers were chastised, and someone realized they could avoid that problem by fetching an updated root CA on demand. They did it over HTTP to avoid a chicken and egg problem.In hardware manufacturing, everything is about crossing items off the list of problems. A problem was raised, someone came up with an idea to solve that problem, and it was implemented. The practice might have spread to other products because it became institutional knowledge about how to avoid a problem that made a customer angry once.This is from my experience in the consumer hardware industry. If you're not watching the outsourced development closely, they will take the easiest route to solve the problem in front of them and nobody will consider any other consequences.reply
Probably something like “What if the cert expires?”reply

did firmware a long time. had two PIs try to force this on me for an IoT device. i pushed back and we missed a deadline. but it uses aws iot certs correctly in a secure element. the customer knew better and thanked me later, lead to 1099 workreply

3rd party SDK requires TLS and it's not easy to bypass. Development contract doesn't allow long-term support where they can push updates if/when proper CA bundle changes.Solution: ignore security in 1st party code outside 3rd party library that tries to prevent ignoring security.As far as I know, most of this cheap crap is basically supply chain management companies that contract a factory to manufacturer and contract a software development/IoT/chip company to write software. Everything is waterfall-style locked in with no ongoing support or funding after the production run is done. The software company doesn't care insomuch as it "works" and working to the SCM company is "powers on and functions", not "is secure". As such, there's not much accountability. If the endeavour gets bad publicity, they just close up shop and spin up a new brand.reply

In general, all synthesizers are distractions from the essentials of music: listening and performing. They replace that with poking around at knobs and setting modes and it does give results, but it can feel really ungrounded when you haven't trained to get any of it to go through your hands directly. JEPA is very similar to Model Predictive Control. Here, you swap the model of the system with black-box simulator (a neural net), apply some version of dynamic programming / Bellman equation to find the optimal action over planning horizon.In the planning stage, by factoring out the optimization step from the rollout step, you can free the model to focus on learning the dynamics in latent space. (The other case, where the rollout+optimization happen in the learning loop, just becomes model-free RL.)My background straddles classical & data-driven controls. Classical control objectives are quite simple, drive the state to stable, follow a trajectory, stay safe. It's very deterministic: Sensor data is used to determine state. State is used to update dynamics, dynamics is used for the forward horizon.So. MPC works for things like self-driving because the car model is fairly knowable and world model is predictable (rules of the road, knowable dynamics of other cars).JEPA seems like a fusion of control, sensing, world model into an embedding space where the learning that occurs is a model free approach to how these are all related to each other.reply
